content: Sieving the resulting white sugar produces various grades that are prepared for commercial sale. There is minimal perceptible difference between sugar derived from sugar beets and that obtained from sugarcane. However, specific tests can distinguish between the two. Some of these tests are designed to detect fraudulent misuse of European Union subsidies or to identify adulteration in fruit juices. The production of sugar generates residues that vary significantly depending on the raw materials used and the location of production. While sugarcane molasses is often used in culinary applications, molasses derived from sugar beets is generally considered unpalatable for human consumption. As a result, beet molasses is primarily utilized as feedstock for industrial fermentation or as animal feed. Once dried, both types of molasses can also serve as fuel for combustion. So-called raw sugars are yellow to brown sugars produced by clarifying the source syrup through boiling and drying with heat, resulting in a crystalline solid with minimal chemical processing. Raw beet sugars are intermediate products in the processing of sugar beet juice, on their way to becoming white sugar. Examples of raw sugar types include demerara, muscovado, and turbinado. Countries like Mauritius and Malawi export significant quantities of these specialty sugars. Manufacturers sometimes prepare raw sugar in loaf form rather than as crystalline powder by combining sugar and molasses in molds and allowing the mixture to dry. This process produces sugar cakes or loaves, known as jaggery or gur in India, pingbian tang in China, and panela, panocha, piloncillo, or pão-de-açúcar in various parts of Latin America. In South America, truly raw sugar, which is unheated and made directly from farm-grown sugarcane, holds a relatively small market share. Mill white sugar, also referred to as plantation white, crystal sugar, or superior sugar, is a type of raw sugar where colored impurities are not removed but instead bleached white using sulfur dioxide. This form of sugar is common in sugarcane-growing regions but does not store or transport well, as its impurities can lead to discoloration and clumping after a few weeks. Blanco directo, a white sugar commonly found in India and other South Asian countries, is produced by precipitating impurities from cane juice using phosphatation, a process involving phosphoric acid and calcium hydroxide, similar to the carbonatation technique used in beet sugar refining. In terms of sucrose purity, blanco directo is purer than mill white sugar but less pure than refined white sugar. White refined sugar has become the most prevalent form of sugar in North America and Europe. It is produced by dissolving raw sugar and purifying it through methods such as phosphoric acid treatment, carbonatation (using calcium hydroxide and carbon dioxide), or various filtration techniques. Further purification is achieved by filtering the sugar through activated carbon or bone char, depending on the processing location. Beet sugar refineries produce refined white sugar directly without an intermediate raw stage. Refined white sugar is typically sold as granulated sugar, which is dried to prevent clumping. Granulated sugar is available in various crystal sizes for different applications, such as coarse-grained sugars like sanding sugar (also known as nibbed sugar or sugar nibs) for decorating cookies and desserts. Powdered sugar, also known as confectioners' sugar, is produced by grinding sugar into a fine powder. Manufacturers may add a small amount of anti-caking agents, such as cornstarch (1–3%) or tricalcium phosphate, to prevent clumping. Retailers also sell sugar cubes or lumps for convenient consumption in standardized amounts. Sugar cubes are made by mixing sugar crystals with sugar syrup. Jakub Kryštof Rad invented sugar cubes in 1841. Brown sugars are produced during the later stages of sugar refining, either by forming fine crystals with significant molasses content or by coating refined white sugar with a cane molasses syrup. The color and flavor of brown sugars intensify with increasing molasses content, as do their moisture-retaining properties. However, brown sugars tend to harden when exposed to air, although proper handling can reverse this. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) define free sugars as all monosaccharides and disaccharides added to foods by manufacturers, cooks, or consumers, as well as sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, and fruit juices. This definition encompasses all the sugars mentioned above. The term free sugars distinguishes these forms from other culinary sugars added in their natural, unrefined state. Natural sugars refer to completely unrefined sugars, effectively all sugars not classified as free sugars. The WHO Technical Report Series 916 on Diet, Nutrition, and the Prevention of Chronic Diseases approves only natural sugars as carbohydrates for unrestricted consumption. Natural sugars are found in fruits, grains, and vegetables in their natural or cooked forms. From a biochemical perspective, sugars are relatively simple carbohydrates. They include monosaccharides, disaccharides, trisaccharides, and oligosaccharides, which contain one, two, three, or more monosaccharide units, respectively. Sugars contain either aldehyde groups (-CHO) or ketone groups (C=O), characterized by carbon-oxygen double bonds, making them chemically reactive. Most simple sugars (monosaccharides) conform to the general formula (CH2O)n, where n ranges from 3 to 7. A notable exception is deoxyribose, which lacks one oxygen atom, as its name suggests. Saccharides with more than one ring in their structure result from two or more monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds, with the loss of one water molecule (H2O) per bond. Chemists classify sugars based on their reactive groups and may further subdivide them according to the number of carbon atoms they contain. Derivatives of trioses (C3H6O3) serve as intermediates in glycolysis.
